tour.description: pyproject.toml defines the 'flights' package (v0.10.0) with its dependencies, optional MCP extras, and three console-script entry points: fli (CLI), fli-mcp (STDIO server), and fli-mcp-http (HTTP server). It also configures the Ruff linter and the Hatchling build system. Understanding the entry points here clarifies how the three interfaces -- CLI, MCP, and library API -- are wired together before diving into each layer.
tour.languageLesson: Python pyproject.toml uses [project.scripts] to define console entry points. Each entry maps a command name to a module:function path (e.g., fli-mcp-http = 'fli.mcp._entry:run_http'). Tools like pip and uv create wrapper scripts that call these functions when the user types the command.

tour.title: Data Model Foundation: Airports and Airlines
tour.description: The Airport and Airline enums form the vocabulary of the entire codebase. Airport catalogs 7,800+ IATA-coded airports with city and country metadata. Airline catalogs 2,200+ IATA airline codes with full names. These enums are generated from CSV data (see Step 12) and are used throughout the search engine for input validation, API encoding, and result display.
tour.languageLesson: Python StrEnum (from the standard library) combines string comparison with enum type safety. Each member is both a string (usable wherever a str is expected) and an enum member (providing exhaustiveness checking in match statements). This pattern is ideal for IATA codes where the set of valid values is known and finite.

tour.title: Google Flights Domain Models and Filters
tour.description: The fli/models/google_flights/ directory defines the Pydantic models that represent the Google Flights API's data structures. base.py contains core enums (SeatType, SortBy, TripType, MaxStops, Alliance) and result types (FlightResult, FlightLeg, FlightSegment, BookingOption, Layover). flights.py and dates.py define FlightSearchFilters and DateSearchFilters -- Pydantic models that validate, serialize, and encode search parameters into the protobuf structure consumed by Google's API. These filter objects are the central data structure that every other layer builds or consumes.
tour.languageLesson: Pydantic models provide runtime validation and serialization with zero boilerplate. Field-level validators (e.g., ensuring departure dates aren't in the past) run automatically on construction. The model's model_dump() and custom encoding methods serialize the validated data into protobuf-compatible dictionaries for the Google Flights API.

tour.title: Core Utilities: Parsing and Building
tour.description: The fli/core/ layer provides shared utilities used by both the CLI and MCP interfaces. parsers.py converts user-facing string inputs (airline codes, alliances like 'ONEWORLD', cabin class names, time ranges like '06-22') into the strongly-typed enums and filter objects from Step 4. builders.py constructs FlightSegment objects for single-leg, multi-city, and date-range search patterns, normalizing dates and assembling time restrictions. Together they form the translation layer between human input and machine-readable API parameters.
tour.languageLesson: The parser layer uses a consistent resolve_enum() pattern: accept a string or comma-separated list, split and strip, then look up each token in the target enum. Invalid values raise ParseError with a message listing valid options. This centralized parsing prevents each CLI command and MCP tool from duplicating input validation logic.

tour.title: HTTP Client and Rate Limiting
tour.description: The search client (client.py) is the gateway to Google Flights' API. It uses curl-cffi for browser impersonation, manages cookies across requests, and wraps all HTTP errors into the typed exception hierarchy from exceptions.py (SearchClientError, SearchTimeoutError, SearchHTTPError). The _concurrency.py module provides a TokenBucketRateLimiter (enforcing 10 requests/second) and a parallel_map utility that fans out search chunks across a thread pool.
tour.languageLesson: The token bucket algorithm maintains a fixed capacity of tokens that refill at a steady rate. Each request consumes one token; if the bucket is empty, the caller blocks until a token becomes available. This provides burst tolerance (short spikes above the average rate) while enforcing a long-term rate limit -- critical for avoiding Google Flights 429 errors.

tour.title: Flight Search Engine
tour.description: SearchFlights (flights.py) is the core search implementation. It builds a FlightSearchFilters object from user parameters, encodes it into Google's protobuf request format, sends it via the HTTP client from Step 6, then feeds the streaming wire-format response through _wire.py (chunked JSON parsing) and _decoders.py (mapping raw JSON into FlightResult Pydantic models). It also generates booking deep-links using _proto.py (tfs token encoding) and retrieves per-vendor booking options.
tour.languageLesson: Google Flights' API returns data in a newline-delimited streaming format where each line is a length-prefixed JSON chunk. _wire.py parses this by reading the hex length header, extracting the JSON payload, and yielding parsed objects. This streaming approach means the client can start processing results before the entire response is received -- important for large result sets where full buffering would add latency.

tour.title: Date Search Engine
tour.description: SearchDates (dates.py) finds the cheapest travel dates within a flexible date range. It partitions the date window into API-compatible chunks and uses the parallel_map utility from Step 6 to execute them concurrently. Each chunk's results are decoded into DatePrice objects, aggregated, and optionally sorted by price. This is the engine behind the 'search_dates' tool that lets users find the best time to fly without checking every date manually.
tour.languageLesson: Date search uses a divide-and-conquer approach: the Google Flights API limits how many dates can be queried in a single request, so SearchDates splits a wide range (e.g., 30 days) into smaller chunks, sends them in parallel via a thread pool, and merges the results. The parallel_map utility ensures the total concurrency stays within the rate limit from Step 6.

tour.title: CLI Interface
tour.description: The CLI (cli/main.py) builds a Typer application with four subcommands: flights, dates, multi (multi-city), and airports. It uses smart argument routing so users can type 'fli JFK LHR 2026-07-15' without explicitly naming the 'flights' subcommand. cli/utils.py provides shared utilities for the CLI layer: parameter validators, date/time normalization, flight/date result serialization to JSON, and Rich-based tabular display with price charts.
tour.languageLesson: Typer is a Python CLI framework built on Click's internals but leveraging type hints. Each command is a decorated function whose parameters automatically become CLI options and arguments. Type annotations drive validation (e.g., Optional[str] becomes an optional flag), and docstrings become help text -- eliminating the duplication between code and CLI definition.

tour.title: MCP Server for AI Integration
tour.description: The MCP server (mcp/server.py) wraps the search engine from Steps 7-8 into a FastMCP-compatible server exposing four tools: search_flights, search_dates, get_booking_options, and find_airports. It defines Pydantic parameter models (FlightSearchParams, DateSearchParams) for input validation, serializes FlightResult objects into JSON-safe dicts for tool responses, and includes two prompt templates for guided AI interactions. The _entry.py module provides the console-script entry points for both STDIO and HTTP transports.
tour.languageLesson: FastMCP (the Python MCP SDK) uses decorators to register tools: @mcp.tool() turns a function into a callable tool exposed over the MCP protocol. Parameter type hints become JSON Schema for client-side validation. The server can run over STDIO (for local Claude Desktop integration) or HTTP (for remote deployment), with _entry.py dispatching to the correct transport based on which entry point is invoked.

tour.title: TypeScript Implementation (fli-js)
tour.description: fli-js is a parallel TypeScript implementation of the Fli library, providing the same Google Flights API access for JavaScript/TypeScript consumers. It mirrors the Python architecture: core/ (parsers, builders, airports), models/ (Airport/Airline enums, Zod-schema filter models), and search/ (HTTP client, rate limiter, flight/date search, protobuf encoding). The package is published independently to npm under the name 'fli-js'.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript's Zod library provides runtime schema validation analogous to Python's Pydantic. Zod schemas are defined as composable objects (z.object({...})), and calling .parse() on input data either returns the validated result or throws a typed ZodError. The fli-js package uses Zod to validate filter parameters before encoding them for the Google Flights API, matching the Python side's Pydantic-based validation.

tour.title: Reference Data and Code Generation
tour.description: The data/ directory contains airports.csv (7,884 airports worldwide with IATA codes, names, cities, countries, and coordinates) and airlines.csv (airline IATA codes mapped to full names). The scripts/generate_enums.py script reads these CSVs and emits the Python enum modules from Step 3. The same CSV data feeds the TypeScript code generator (fli-js/scripts/generate-enums.ts), ensuring both language implementations share identical reference data.

tour.title: Containerization and Deployment
tour.description: The Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build: a builder stage installs dependencies with uv, then a minimal runtime stage copies only the virtual environment and runs fli-mcp-http as a non-root user on port 8000. docker-compose.yml adds health checks and automatic restart. The Makefile provides development automation targets (install, test, lint, docs, release). Together these let the MCP server run in production with minimal attack surface.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use multiple FROM statements. The first stage (builder) has full dev tooling for compilation; the final stage copies only the compiled artifacts. This keeps the production image small (only runtime dependencies) and secure (no compilers or dev tools accessible to attackers). Layer ordering matters: rarely-changing layers (OS packages, Python) go first so Docker's build cache can skip them on repeated builds.

tour.title: CI/CD and Release Automation
tour.description: GitHub Actions orchestrates the full quality and release pipeline. ci.yml runs lint (Ruff), tests (pytest across Python 3.10-3.13), and type checking on every push and PR. release.yml and release-npm.yml manage independent version bumps and publishing for the Python (PyPI) and TypeScript (npm) packages. The scripts/bump_version.py utility handles semantic version computation for both ecosystems, keeping the release process consistent across languages.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use 'on' triggers (push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch for manual runs) and 'jobs' for parallel execution units. The release workflows use a 'dry_run' input parameter to preview the version bump before committing -- a safety pattern that prevents accidental releases. The CI matrix strategy (testing across Python 3.10-3.13) catches version-specific regressions before they reach users.

tour.title: Documentation Site
tour.description: The docs/ directory builds a complete documentation site with MkDocs Material theme. docs/index.md serves as the homepage with key features and quick-start snippets. docs/guides/mcp.md provides a comprehensive MCP Server guide covering installation, STDIO and HTTP modes, Claude Desktop configuration, and all four MCP tools with parameter tables. Understanding this documentation layer shows how the project communicates its capabilities to users and AI assistants, completing the tour from code internals to user-facing surface.
tour.languageLesson: MkDocs with the Material theme and mkdocstrings plugin automatically generates API reference pages from Python docstrings. Google-style docstrings (Args:, Returns:, Raises:) are parsed into structured documentation, so the same docstrings that help developers in-editor also populate the public docs site. This eliminates the drift between code and documentation that plagues manually-maintained API references.
